title: Saturday Expense Recap
topic: Two equal card charges that were not an even split
blurb: After the concert and hotpot, one friend sent a note to settle up.
prompt: A friend asked an AI to write this settle-up note. If a line doesn't add up, tap it.

segments.label: The ticket
segments.text: I bought your $120 concert ticket online; I already had mine from work, so that charge was just for you.

segments.label: The dinner
segments.text: After the show you paid the $120 hotpot bill for the two of us.

segments.label: The settlement
segments.text: We each put $120 on our cards, so we're completely even — no transfer needed.

segments.label: The tone
segments.text: Thanks again for a fun Saturday; let's do another night next month.

segments.label: The close
segments.text: I'll mark the weekend as settled in our chat.

conclusion: AI note: both people spent $120, so the weekend is already even. No transfer needed.

flaws.original: The $120 ticket was entirely for you, while the $120 dinner was shared ($60 each). I covered $120 of your costs and you covered $60 of mine, so you still owe me $60.
flaws.corrupted: We each put $120 on our cards, so we're completely even — no transfer needed.

diagnosis_choices.label: Equal card charges are not an even split when one bill was for one person and the other bill was shared.
The hotpot bill should have been split three ways, including the waiter.
A work-issued ticket has no cash value, so only the dinner needs to be settled.
You actually owe $120 more, because concert tickets can be resold.

fix_choices.label: I covered your whole $120 ticket and half the dinner; you covered only $60 of my dinner. You still owe $60.
Keep it as even: matching totals on two cards always cancel.
Split both bills in half, so each person owes $120 and the transfer is $0.
Ignore the ticket and split only the hotpot, which already makes the $120 charges even.

flaws.explanation: Spending the same amount only makes you even when you shared both bills. One friend covered the other's whole ticket ($120) and received only half a dinner ($60) in return — a $60 gap.
flaws.why_tempting: Two identical $120 charges look like a clean swap, so it's easy to skip who each bill was actually for.
flaws.catch_rule: Before calling a split even, check which costs were personal and which were shared — matching totals are not enough.
flaws.hint: Of the $120 dinner, how much was for each person? What about the ticket?

practice.problem: You pay a $40 taxi for both of you; your friend pays a $40 museum ticket that is only for you. Even?
practice.answer: No. They covered $40 of your costs; you covered $20 of theirs. You still owe $20.

clean_segments: I bought your $120 concert ticket online; I already had mine from work, so that charge was just for you.
After the show you paid the $120 hotpot bill for the two of us.
I covered your whole $120 ticket and $60 of the dinner; you covered $60 of my dinner. You still owe $60.
Thanks again for a fun Saturday; let's do another night next month.
I'll send a $60 transfer request in the chat.
clean_conclusion: Matching $120 charges are not an even split: one bill was personal, the other was shared. $60 is still owed.
